prompt: What other proteins are related to histones, and describe that relationship using SCOPe classification levels.
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, nucleosome core histones belong to the all-alpha class a, Histone-fold fold a.22 (SUNID 47112), Histone-fold superfamily a.22.1 (SUNID 47113), and Nucleosome core histones family a.22.1.1 (SUNID 47114). H2A, H2B, H3, H4, and the histone domain of macro-H2A.1 are members of that same family, so SCOPe supports the closest, family-level relationship among their classified domains.

Other probable homologs occur in separate families of the same a.22.1 superfamily: (1) archaeal histones, family a.22.1.2 (SUNID 47129); (2) the TBP-associated-factor family a.22.1.3 (SUNID 47134), comprising TAFII42, TAFII62, TAFII18, TAFII28, the histone-fold domains of TAF4/TAFII135 and TAF12/TAFII20, NF-YB, NF-YC, NC2 alpha and beta, CHRAC-14, CHRAC-16, and the histone domain of Son of sevenless; and (3) bacterial histone-fold proteins, family a.22.1.4 (SUNID 101318), including Aq_328 and TTHA1479. Because these families share superfamily 47113 but not family 47114, SCOPe supports probable common ancestry with core histones, but a more remote relationship than that among core-family members. SCOPe annotates the bacterial family as a duplication of two histone-fold repeats arranged like the subunits of an archaeal histone dimer, with the 1wws structure forming dimers resembling an H3-H4 tetramer.

SCOPe also has a.22.1.0 (SUNID 238448) under this superfamily for automated matches, but its explicit annotation says “not a true family”; those entries should therefore be reported as automated superfamily placements, not used as evidence of ordinary family-level relatedness.

Names alone are misleading: linker histones H1/H5 are classified instead in the DNA/RNA-binding three-helical-bundle fold, winged-helix superfamily, family a.4.5.13 (SUNID 46827), while H-NS “histone-like” proteins are in their own fold and superfamily, family a.155.1.1 (SUNID 81272). They share only the broad all-alpha class with a.22 histones; SCOPe therefore does not assert histone-superfamily homology for them. Likewise, enzymes named for modifying histones are not thereby histone homologs.

These classifications apply to domains, not necessarily entire multidomain proteins. Superfamily membership does not justify transferring nucleosome assembly, DNA-binding mode, transcriptional function, partner specificity, oligomeric state, or ligand/substrate specificity, nor does it make the proteins interchangeable structural templates. Stronger functional or mechanistic claims require sequence correspondence, global structural alignment, interface or ligand/partner-bound structures, compatible domain context, biochemical experiments, phylogenetic analysis, and supporting literature. Conversely, different folds or superfamilies mean only that SCOPe makes no positive homology assertion; they do not prove convergence or independent origin.

prompt: What evolutionary relationship does SCOPe support between the MazG-like domain d1vmga_ and the HisE-like domain d1y6xa1, and what functional conclusions would go beyond that evidence?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, d1vmga_ (SUNID 113676) is in the MazG-like family a.204.1.2 (SUNID 116993), whereas d1y6xa1 (SUNID 122676; residues A:7–93) is in the HisE-like (PRA-PH) family a.204.1.4 (SUNID 140797). They are therefore not members of the same family, but both belong to the all-alpha NTP pyrophosphatases superfamily a.204.1 (SUNID 101386), within fold a.204 and class a. Their deepest shared homology-bearing level is the superfamily, so SCOPe supports probable common ancestry—a remote homologous relationship—despite their family-level divergence. The shared fold and class describe broader structural organization; the positive evolutionary inference comes from the shared superfamily.

This placement does not justify transferring the HisE annotation to d1vmga_: it does not show that d1vmga_ catalyzes phosphoribosyl-ATP hydrolysis or participates in histidine biosynthesis. Nor does it justify assigning MazG-family substrate preference, reaction chemistry, pathway role, ligand specificity, catalytic residues, regulation, or oligomeric behavior to d1y6xa1. It also does not make the structures interchangeable templates for active-site, ligand-binding, or functional modeling; at most, either may be a candidate remote structural template for the conserved core. Stronger functional or template claims require external evidence such as a domain-level structural alignment with adequate coverage, sequence and active-site correspondence in equivalent structural positions, ligand-bound structures, biochemical substrate/reaction assays, suitable structure-quality data, compatible domain architecture and genomic context, phylogenetic analysis, and supporting literature.

prompt: Actin/HSP70, hexokinase, and glycerol kinase have very different cellular roles. What relationship does SCOPe place among their catalytic domains, and what does that relationship permit you to infer?
answer: In stable SCOPe 2.08, the catalytic domains belong to separate families—Actin/HSP70 c.55.1.1 (SUNID 53068), Hexokinase c.55.1.3 (SUNID 53083), and Glycerol kinase c.55.1.4 (SUNID 53089)—within the same Actin-like ATPase domain superfamily c.55.1 (SUNID 53067). They also share the Ribonuclease H-like motif fold c.55 (SUNID 53066) and alpha/beta class c (SUNID 51349). Thus, SCOPe supports probable common ancestry among these domains; actin and HSP70 have the closer, shared-family placement. The superfamily annotation additionally notes a duplication containing two domains of this fold. This placement does not permit transfer of exact substrate specificity, reaction chemistry, cellular role, regulation, kinetics, oligomeric state, or whole-protein function, nor does it make representatives interchangeable templates. Those stronger conclusions require domain-level sequence and structural alignments, conserved active-site residues in equivalent structural contexts, ligand-bound structures, domain-architecture analysis, phylogenetic evidence, and biochemical experiments.

prompt: How should the relationship among ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins, and manganese catalases be interpreted from SCOPe, given their different chemistries?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, these are three distinct families within the same homology-bearing Ferritin-like superfamily: Ferritin (SUNID 47241; a.25.1.1), Ribonucleotide reductase-like (SUNID 47253; a.25.1.2), and Manganese catalase/T-catalase (SUNID 100951; a.25.1.3). All descend from Ferritin-like superfamily SUNID 47240 (a.25.1), so SCOPe supports probable common ancestry despite their divergent chemistries. They also share Ferritin-like fold SUNID 47239 (a.25) in the all-alpha class; SCOPe describes its core as a closed, left-handed four-helix bundle with one crossover and annotates the superfamily as containing a bimetal-ion center in the bundle.

The family split is biologically important: canonical ferritins perform iron oxidation/mineralization and storage, ribonucleotide-reductase R2-like proteins support radical chemistry for nucleotide reduction, and manganese catalases disproportionate hydrogen peroxide. Superfamily membership supports descent and reuse of a structural/metal-binding scaffold, not transfer of exact reaction, substrate, metal identity, oxidation state, radical mechanism, active-site residues, oligomeric assembly, or whole-protein function. In particular, the label “ribonucleotide reductase-like” does not establish that every member performs the canonical R2 reaction. A member of one family is therefore only a remote scaffold-level template for another, not an interchangeable functional or active-site template; no best representative can be selected here because structure-quality records were not compared. Stronger mechanistic transfer would require family-resolved sequence and structural alignments, conservation of ligating/catalytic residues in equivalent positions, metal- or ligand-bound structures, biochemical assays of metals/substrates/products and kinetics, and ideally phylogenetic and domain-context evidence.

prompt: Plastocyanin/azurin-like proteins, ephrin ectodomains, and the N-terminal domain of PAD4 appear biologically unrelated. What does SCOPe say about their relationship, and should copper binding or electron transfer be inferred across them?
answer: No copper-binding or electron-transfer function should be transferred across these groups. In stable SCOPe 2.08, their classified domains share the homology-bearing Cupredoxins superfamily, b.6.1 (SUNID 49503), within the Cupredoxin-like fold b.6 (SUNID 49502) and all-beta class b (SUNID 48724). They are nevertheless separate families: Plastocyanin/azurin-like b.6.1.1 (SUNID 49504), Ephrin ectodomain b.6.1.5 (SUNID 74874), and the PAD4 N-terminal domain b.6.1.6 (SUNID 110107). Thus SCOPe supports probable common ancestry of these domains—stronger than fold-level resemblance—but not close family membership or biochemical equivalence; this domain relationship also does not make their whole proteins functionally interchangeable. Although the shared superfamily has the comment “contains copper-binding site,” the more specific ephrin annotation calls it a eukaryotic signaling domain related to cupredoxins but lacking the metal-binding site, and the PAD4 N-terminal-family annotation likewise says it lacks that site. Nothing retrieved establishes electron transfer for either family. Such assignments would require external residue-level sequence and structural comparisons demonstrating conserved copper-coordination geometry, copper-bound structural or spectroscopic evidence, direct metal-binding and redox/electron-transfer assays, and compatible domain-context or functional literature. Conversely, ephrin signaling and PAD4-associated functions should not be transferred to plastocyanin/azurin-like domains from superfamily membership alone.

prompt: What biologically useful relationship does SCOPe support among ubiquitin-related proteins, UBX domains, and Ras-binding domains, and what annotation transfer would be unsafe?
answer: In stable SCOPe 2.08, Ubiquitin-related proteins (family d.15.1.1, SUNID 54237), UBX domains (d.15.1.2, SUNID 54250), and Ras-binding domains/RBDs (d.15.1.5, SUNID 54263) are distinct families within the same Ubiquitin-like superfamily (d.15.1, SUNID 54236) and beta-Grasp fold (d.15, SUNID 54235). Their deepest shared homology-bearing level is therefore the superfamily, so SCOPe supports probable common ancestry and a conserved beta-grasp structural core despite substantial functional divergence. This is useful for remote-homology analysis and cautious core-structure comparison; it does not make the domains functionally equivalent or automatically interchangeable as modeling templates for binding surfaces or complexes. Unsafe transfers include assigning ubiquitin conjugation, proteasomal-tag, or other ubiquitin-specific activity to UBX or RBD domains; assigning Ras-family GTPase binding/signaling to ubiquitin-related or UBX domains; or assigning UBX-specific adaptor interactions such as p97/VCP binding to the other families. Such functions require family- and protein-specific evidence—sequence conservation at relevant sites, domain architecture, structural alignment and preferably complex/ligand-bound structures, biochemical interaction or activity assays, and phylogenetic or literature support.

prompt: CheY-related response regulators, an ornithine-decarboxylase N-terminal wing, and the KaiA N-terminal domain share a structural lineage in SCOPe. What relationship is supported, and which signaling or catalytic claims are not?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, the CheY-related family (SUNID 52173; c.23.1.1), ornithine-decarboxylase N-terminal “wing” family (SUNID 52252; c.23.1.4), and KaiA N-terminal-domain family (SUNID 82344; c.23.1.5) are distinct families within the CheY-like superfamily (SUNID 52172; c.23.1), itself in the flavodoxin-like fold (SUNID 52171; c.23). Their deepest shared classification is therefore a homology-bearing superfamily: SCOPe supports probable remote common ancestry of the classified domains, not merely similar topology, but does not place them in one close family.

That relationship does not transfer CheY-family two-component signaling, receiver-domain phosphorylation, phosphoacceptor/metal-binding chemistry, conformational switching, or interaction partners to the ornithine-decarboxylase wing or KaiA N-terminal domain. Indeed, SCOPe annotates the KaiA family as lacking canonical receiver-domain features. Conversely, the classification does not show that CheY-related or KaiA domains bind PLP, decarboxylate ornithine, share an ornithine-decarboxylase active site, or that the N-terminal wing is itself the catalytic module. Nor does it transfer KaiA circadian-clock function to the other families. Whole-protein functions, substrates, pathways, and exact mechanisms cannot be inferred from this domain-level superfamily placement.

The shared superfamily can motivate a remote-homology/core-structure template, but not an interchangeable functional or whole-protein template. Stronger signaling claims require sequence and structure comparisons of equivalent receiver residues, phosphorylated or metal-bound structures, phosphotransfer assays, interaction data, and domain-context evidence. Catalytic claims require active-site and cofactor comparisons, ligand/substrate-bound structures, full enzyme-architecture evidence, and direct biochemical activity or kinetic assays.

prompt: Why is the bulge domain of the V1 ATP synthase A subunit classified separately from the other barrel-sandwich-hybrid superfamilies, and what evolutionary claim does that placement make?
answer: In stable SCOPe 2.08, the V1 ATP synthase A-subunit bulge is family b.84.5.1 (SUNID 310616) within its own superfamily, b.84.5 “V1 ATP synthase A subunit, bulge domain-like” (SUNID 310577). For example, domain d3gqba3 (3gqb A:113–184; SUNID 305428) has that lineage. b.84.5 shares the Barrel-sandwich hybrid fold b.84 (SUNID 51229)—described as a sandwich of half-barrel-shaped beta sheets—with four separately curated superfamilies: b.84.1 Single hybrid motif, b.84.2 Rudiment single hybrid motif, b.84.3 Duplicated hybrid motif, and b.84.4 Ribosomal L27 protein-like. Thus SCOPe recognizes a common fold-level architecture but confines its positive homology assertion for the bulge domains to b.84.5; the fold record explicitly says that levels above superfamily do not imply homology. The separate placement therefore means SCOPe does not assert superfamily-level common ancestry between the ATP-synthase bulge and b.84.1–b.84.4. It does not positively establish convergence, independent origins, analogy, or proven nonhomology. Nor may ATP-synthase function, motifs, or interchangeable-template status be transferred between these superfamilies from the fold match alone. The API exposes the placement and a b.84.5 annotation citing PubMed 19893485, but not the detailed curatorial argument. A stronger evolutionary explanation would require inspection of that paper plus global structural alignment/topology, core-sequence or equivalent-position motif correspondence, compatible domain context, and phylogenetic or experimental evidence.

prompt: Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes, fumarate-reductase respiratory-complex transmembrane subunits, and respiratory nitrate-reductase gamma chains all use a heme-binding four-helical-bundle architecture. Does SCOPe support treating them as one homologous superfamily?
answer: No. In stable SCOPe 2.08, these are three separate superfamilies: transmembrane di-heme cytochromes (f.21.1, SUNID 81342), fumarate-reductase respiratory-complex transmembrane subunits (f.21.2, SUNID 81343), and respiratory nitrate-reductase 1 gamma chains (f.21.3, SUNID 103501). Their deepest shared classification is the heme-binding four-helical-bundle fold (f.21, SUNID 81344) in class f, “Membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides” (SUNID 56835). Thus SCOPe supports a shared four-transmembrane-helix topology, not one homologous family or superfamily. The f.21 fold annotation describes an up-and-down four-helix bundle binding one or two hemes, while its homology record explicitly says levels above superfamily do not imply homology. The nitrate-reductase gamma-chain annotation does note a possible link between the other two superfamilies and structural closeness to FrdC, but SCOPe still retains it as a distinct superfamily; that comment is suggestive, not a merged homology assignment. Conversely, separate superfamilies do not prove convergence, independent origin, or biological nonhomology. It would be unsafe to transfer exact heme-ligation geometry, electron-transfer function, substrate specificity, complex role, or interchangeable-template status among the three groups from the fold alone. A stronger evolutionary or template claim requires external global structural alignments, core-sequence correspondence and conserved motifs in equivalent structural contexts, compatible membrane/domain architecture, phylogenetic or literature support, and biochemical or ligand-bound evidence for functional transfer.

prompt: How should a biologist interpret SCOPe's relationship among alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains, CoA-binding domains, and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, the alcohol-dehydrogenase-like C-terminal domains (family c.2.1.1, SUNID 51736), CoA-binding domains (c.2.1.8, SUNID 51900), and potassium-channel NAD-binding domains (c.2.1.9, SUNID 63944) are distinct families within the same NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily c.2.1 (SUNID 51735). All also lie in fold c.2 (SUNID 51734) and class c, whose retrieved fold annotation describes a three-layer α/β/α core with a six-stranded parallel β-sheet in order 321456. The shared superfamily—not merely the shared fold—means SCOPe supports probable common ancestry of their classified domains; their separation into three families represents substantial specialization and does not support a closer, same-family relationship.

Function must not be transferred across these families from their names alone. In particular, alcohol-dehydrogenase reaction chemistry or substrate specificity cannot be assigned to the CoA-binding or channel-associated domains; CoA binding cannot be assigned to the other two; and NAD binding, ion-channel regulation, or whole potassium-channel function cannot be assigned outside c.2.1.9. The c.2.1.1 annotation additionally says that an N-terminal all-beta domain defines that family, so its C-terminal Rossmann domain alone does not establish the complete alcohol-dehydrogenase architecture or function. The c.2.1.9 annotation records an automatic mapping to Pfam PF02254; this is provenance, not biochemical validation or evidence of low quality.

The shared superfamily can justify considering remote structural templates for the conserved Rossmann core, but not treating family members as interchangeable templates for ligand-binding residues, loops, insertions, oligomerization, catalytic sites, or regulatory interfaces. Stronger functional transfer requires target-specific sequence and core-position correspondence, active-site or ligand-contact conservation in equivalent structural contexts, ligand-bound structural evidence, compatible domain architecture, and biochemical binding or catalytic assays; detailed evolutionary claims may also require phylogenetic and literature evidence. SCOPe hierarchy alone also cannot select a best representative: quality records for every candidate and the relevant ligand, conformational, and biological states would be required.

prompt: In SCOPe 2.08, are d1s9za_ (Amyloidogenic design-1) and d1hqja_ (Unnamed design-1) homologous?
answer: Homology is not established. In SCOPe 2.08, d1s9za_ (Amyloidogenic design-1; SUNID 98768) and d1hqja_ (Unnamed design-1; SUNID 61142) share designed-protein class k, fold k.40, superfamily k.40.1, and nominal family k.40.1.1 (SUNID 100905). Ordinarily a shared family would support close homology, but this family is explicitly annotated “not a true family,” so its shared-family placement must not be interpreted as evidence of common evolutionary ancestry. The generic homology endpoint’s level-based flag does not remove that specific caveat. The pair may be compared as designed trimeric coiled-coil structures, but neither should be treated as a close homolog or automatically interchangeable template for the other. In particular, Amyloidogenic design-1’s amyloidogenic behavior must not be transferred to Unnamed design-1, and their respective Na/Zn versus Pb/SIN/SO4 complex annotations do not establish shared ligand specificity or function. A stronger relationship would require external design-provenance or sequence-derivation evidence, sequence and structural alignments, and experimental evidence for aggregation, ligand binding, or other claimed properties.

prompt: Andreeva et al. 2008 describe PA1492 as a classification-change example. How did the relationship between PA1492 (PDB 1t1j) and nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase (PDB 1f8y) change between SCOP 1.69 and the current SCOPe release?
answer:
The current-release metadata designates SCOPe 2.08 as the current stable release; 2.08-2026-08-16 is a periodic update and does not replace that stable release.

In SCOP 1.69, PA1492 from 1t1j was classified in its own fold, superfamily, and family: chain-A domain d1t1ja_ (SUNID 106249; chain B was equivalently classified) had SCCS c.137.1.1. Nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase from 1f8y, represented by d1f8ya_ (SUNID 31395; likewise for chain B), was c.23.14.1: flavodoxin-like fold c.23, N-deoxyribosyltransferase superfamily c.23.14. Their deepest shared level was only class c, so SCOP 1.69 asserted neither a shared fold nor superfamily-level common ancestry. That historical separation is not proof that they were nonhomologous, analogous, or convergently evolved.

In SCOPe 2.08, the PA1492 protein domain is d1t1ja1, residues A:1-118 (same SUNID 106249), classified as c.23.14.2; the chain-B counterpart is classified identically. The 1f8y domains remain c.23.14.1. Thus they now share the flavodoxin-like fold c.23 and, more importantly, the N-(deoxy)ribosyltransferase-like superfamily c.23.14, while remaining in different families: PA1492 c.23.14.2 versus N-deoxyribosyltransferase c.23.14.1. The relationship therefore changed from only same-class placement to a SCOPe-supported probable common ancestry at the superfamily level, not a same-family relationship.

This reclassification does not establish that PA1492 performs the nucleoside 2-deoxyribosyltransferase reaction, accepts 1f8y's substrates or ligand, or shares its exact catalytic residues, specificity, or mechanism. Such transfer would require sequence and structural alignments, active-site correspondence in equivalent structural contexts, ligand-bound structures, and biochemical evidence. The retrieved API records establish the before-and-after classification but do not expose Andreeva et al.'s detailed evidence or the curatorial rationale; verifying why the change was made requires the paper and its supporting structural/sequence evidence.

prompt: SCOPe 2.08 divides PDB 1a14 chain H into d1a14h1 covering residues 9-111 and d1a14h2 covering residues 1-8. What is the second segment, and should similarity to it be treated as protein homology evidence?
answer: In SCOPe 2.08, d1a14h2 (SUNID 343393; residues H:1-8; SCCS l.1.1.1) is a synthetic N-terminal tag: class l “Artifacts,” with Tag fold, superfamily, and family assignments. It is not a second biological protein domain. By contrast, d1a14h1 (SUNID 20061; H:9-111; b.1.1.1) is the immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable domain in the V-set family. SCOPe explicitly marks homology as not implied for d1a14h2 and warns that similarity to class-l artificial-sequence records does not imply biological homology. Therefore, tag matches should be masked or excluded from homology inference and should not be transferred as protein-family annotations or used as biological-domain templates. Any claim that the eight residues derive from a genuine protein relationship would require independent construct/provenance documentation plus sequence or structural evidence involving the biological protein region; similarity to the tag alone is insufficient.

prompt: How did the SCOP 1.75 domain definitions for PDB 1acc chain A change in newer releases of SCOPe? What does the change reveal about domains as evolutionary modules, and how should it affect homology searches?
answer:
SCOP 1.75 classified 1acc chain A as one whole-chain domain, d1acca_ (SUNID 43828; A:; SCCS f.11.1.1, Anthrax protective antigen family). This definition persisted in SCOPe 2.03. In SCOPe 2.04 it was replaced by two domains, a division retained in current stable release 2.08: d1acca1 (SUNID 238521; A:226–735) belongs to class f, fold f.60, superfamily f.60.1, family f.60.1.1 (Anthrax protective antigen C-terminal-like), whereas d1acca2 (SUNID 238522; A:14–225) belongs to all-beta class b, fold b.179, PA14-like superfamily b.179.1, and PA14 family b.179.1.1. Residues 1–13 are outside these newer classified boundaries.

Thus this was not merely an SID rename: a former whole-chain unit was split into two separately classified structural/evolutionary modules. Their different classes and superfamilies mean that SCOPe makes no homology assertion between the two modules; this supports treating them separately but does not prove independent origins or convergence. The API establishes the reclassification, not its curator rationale—explaining why it occurred would require residue-mapped structural superpositions, sequence evidence, domain-context comparisons, or relevant literature.

Homology searches should therefore use the two domain ranges independently and record the SCOPe release. A match to the N-terminal PA14-like domain must not be extended automatically to the C-terminal domain or the whole protein, and vice versa; whole-chain searches could dilute a domain-specific signal or create misleading composite similarity. Structural templates should likewise be selected per domain, while modeling their full-chain arrangement requires separate interface and relative-orientation evidence. Exact function, calcium dependence, ligand specificity, mechanism, or whole-protein function cannot be transferred from family/superfamily membership or from the shared “complexed with Ca” annotation alone; such transfer needs domain-level sequence/structure evidence plus ligand-bound, biochemical, architectural, phylogenetic, or literature support.

prompt: What does SCOPe's five-domain decomposition of Prp8 in PDB 3jb9 reveal about its evolutionary history? Which domains are related to previously characterized proteins, and which represents a newly observed fold?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, Prp8 is chain A of 3jb9 and is decomposed, N-to-C, into five domains. Four have homology-bearing placements among previously characterized protein groups: d3jb9a4 (residues 698–822; a.29.2.1) is in the bromodomain family; d3jb9a3 (823–1604; e.8.1.8) is the Prp8 reverse-transcriptase domain within the DNA/RNA-polymerase superfamily, which also contains conventional reverse transcriptases; d3jb9a2 (1605–1780; c.52.1.36) is a Prp8 endonuclease-like family within the restriction-endonuclease-like superfamily; and d3jb9a1 (1784–2030; c.55.3.14) is the Prp8 beta-finger family within the RNase-H-like superfamily, alongside RNase H, retroviral-integrase, transposase, and resolvase families. Family membership gives the strongest relationship for the bromodomain; the other three are distinct families sharing established superfamilies, supporting probable common ancestry but not identical functions.

The fifth domain, d3jb9a5 (residues 47–697; d.394.1.1), is the large N-terminal Prp8/Spp42 domain. SCOPe assigns it its own fold, d.394 (SUNID 345891), containing only the Prp8/Spp42 superfamily; this is the newly observed fold in the five-domain decomposition.

Thus Prp8 is an evolutionary mosaic: an otherwise novel N-terminal scaffold is joined to bromodomain-, polymerase/RT-, endonuclease-, and RNase-H-like modules. This is compatible with evolutionary accretion around an ancient polymerase/nuclease core and with proposed group-II-intron/retroelement connections, but SCOPe alone does not establish the fusion chronology or that Prp8 retains reverse-transcription, restriction-endonuclease, RNase-H, integrase, or canonical acetyl-lysine-binding activity. Those stronger claims require sequence and structure alignments, active-site and ligand-bound comparisons, biochemical assays, phylogenetic/domain-context analysis, and supporting literature. Likewise, a Prp8-specific fold assignment does not prove de novo origin or absence of undiscovered remote homologs.

prompt: Why do d2kq5a_, d3v6pa_, and d4cj9a_ all belong to TAL effector family a.298.1.1 in SCOPe despite vastly different sequence lengths?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, all three domains have the same family ancestor: TAL (transcription activator-like) effector, a.298.1.1, SUNID 267609. They also share superfamily a.298.1 (TAL effector-like), fold a.298 (left-handed alpha-alpha superhelix), and class a (all-alpha proteins). The domain records identify d2kq5a_ as PthA, d3v6pa_ as dHax3, and d4cj9a_ as BurrH. Thus, their placement is a family-level homology assertion, not merely resemblance at the fold level.

Their different lengths reflect the modular, tandem-repeat nature of TAL effectors. The retrieved observed-ATOM domain sequences are 51 residues for d2kq5a_, 373 for d3v6pa_, and 752 for d4cj9a_. SCOPe explicitly comments that d2kq5a_ is a “single repeat”; d2kq5a_ and d3v6pa_ carry the `re` heterogeneity flag, defined for a family whose domains contain different numbers of small repeating units. The family annotation designates d4cj9a_ residues A:259–292 as the canonical representative repeat. Consequently, repeat-unit ancestry and conserved repeat architecture justify one family even though the classified constructs contain very different numbers of tandem copies; raw total length is not the family-defining criterion.

This classification does not establish identical repeat count, DNA-recognition code or target sequence, host specificity, biological activity, or interchangeability as whole-domain structural templates. Those transfers require repeat-resolved sequence and structural alignments, verified domain boundaries and construct context, plus DNA-bound/ligand-bound structures or biochemical binding and functional evidence. Template selection must also account for coverage and repeat-number compatibility rather than treating the 51-, 373-, and 752-residue domains as equivalent full-length models.

prompt: What stable release and latest periodic update are reported by the current-release endpoint? Which identifier should be cited for a reproducible analysis, and what does the periodic label mean?
answer: The current-release endpoint reports stable release SCOPe 2.08 (`stable_label`: `2.08-stable`) and latest periodic update `2.08-2026-08-16`, dated 2026-08-16. For reproducible analysis, pin the stable release selector `2.08` and cite it as `2.08-stable`; do not cite an unqualified “current” release. The periodic label identifies the dated update associated with the 2.08 baseline, not a replacement stable release. Current-release metadata alone does not establish which records were added or changed in that update; verifying such changes requires release-scoped record comparisons.

prompt: Early structures 1br0 and 1ez3 contained fragments of the syntaxin N-terminal domain, whereas 1dn1 chain B showed the full domain. How should SCOPe's current treatment of these structures change the biological interpretation of fragment-based fold assignments?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, the fragments d1br0a_ and d1ez3a_/d1ez3b_/d1ez3c_, and full-domain structure d1dn1b_, are all assigned to the t-SNARE family a.47.2.1 (SUNID 47662), t-SNARE superfamily a.47.2 (SUNID 47661), STAT-like fold a.47 (SUNID 47654), and all-alpha class a. Thus the deepest common SCOPe level is family, supporting a close relationship among the classified syntaxin regions—not merely a generic three-helix resemblance. The fragments reside under the “Syntaxin 1A N-terminal domain” protein node (SUNID 47663); d1dn1b_ is instead recorded under “automated matches,” with the comment “automated match to d3c98b_,” so SCOPe directly supports their common family placement but not common protein-node membership.

The fragment caveat is essential: SCOPe describes d1br0a_ and every 1ez3 domain as a “three-helical fragment; similar to one spectrin repeat” and marks each ms, meaning secondary structures comprising less than one-third of the common domain are missing. The enclosing STAT-like fold is described as a four-long-helix bundle, whereas the separately classified Spectrin repeat-like fold is a.7 (SUNID 46965), described as a three-helix bundle. Consequently, resemblance of the truncated three-helix core to one spectrin repeat must not be promoted to a whole-domain spectrin-fold assignment, spectrin homology, or spectrin-like function. The complete-domain context supplied by 1dn1 B—and represented currently through its match to d3c98b_—changes the interpretation from “this fragment defines the fold” to “this fragment samples part of a larger t-SNARE/STAT-like domain.” SCOPe 1.75 already gives these entries the same a.47.2.1 placement, so the queried releases do not date an earlier reclassification or reveal its curator rationale.

For structural comparison or template use, 1br0 and 1ez3 should cover only their observed core: absent helices must not be scored as biological deletions, and the fragments are not interchangeable whole-domain templates. A complete-domain structure should anchor global topology and boundary decisions, but d1dn1 is obsolete in favor of 3c98, and no “best” representative can be selected without quality, coverage, conformational-state, and experimental-context evidence for every candidate. Likewise, family membership does not by itself transfer exact SNARE interactions, regulatory state, ligand/partner specificity, or biochemical function; resemblance to a spectrin repeat transfers none of spectrin’s mechanical or cytoskeletal roles. Establishing the detailed reason for the placement—or any relationship to spectrin beyond local shape—would require a complete-domain structural alignment, residue-level sequence correspondence across the full core, compatible domain context, and relevant phylogenetic or experimental/literature evidence. Different SCOPe folds mean that SCOPe makes no positive homology assertion between syntaxin and spectrin; they do not by themselves prove convergence or nonhomology.

prompt: NAD(P)-binding enzymes occur in multiple SCOP folds and superfamilies. What does this imply about convergent versus divergent evolution, and why is cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone insufficient evidence of homology?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, NAD(P)-associated domains occupy demonstrably different classifications: the NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold superfamily c.2.1 (SUNID 51735) is in fold c.2 (SUNID 51734); NAD(P)-linked oxidoreductases c.1.7 (SUNID 51430) are in the TIM beta/alpha-barrel fold c.1 (SUNID 51350); the DHS-like NAD/FAD-binding superfamily c.31.1 (SUNID 52467) is in fold c.31 (SUNID 52466); and the HMG-CoA-reductase NAD-binding superfamily d.58.20 (SUNID 55035) is in the ferredoxin-like fold d.58 (SUNID 54861), even a different SCOP class (d rather than c). SCOPe additionally comments that c.31.1 binds cofactors in the opposite direction from the classical Rossmann fold.

This pattern is compatible with repeated convergent recruitment of NAD(P)-binding chemistry by different structural architectures, but SCOPe hierarchy alone does not prove independent origins or convergence. Within a family, SCOPe supports the closest relationship; within one superfamily, it supports probable common ancestry and subsequent divergent evolution, even when functions differ. Sharing only a fold supports similar topology, not homology, while placement in different folds or superfamilies means SCOPe makes no positive homology assertion between them—not that it proves nonhomology.

Cofactor binding and local active-site similarity are insufficient because NAD/NADP chemistry imposes recurring geometric and electrostatic constraints: short phosphate-binding motifs, glycine-rich loops, or similar catalytic residues can arise independently and represent only a small fraction of a domain. Conversely, homologs may substantially change cofactor specificity, substrates, catalytic residues, or reaction chemistry. Thus NAD versus NADP preference, substrate, reaction, mechanism, residue equivalence, whole-protein function, and interchangeable template status must not be transferred merely from cofactor binding, an active-site resemblance, fold membership, or even superfamily membership.

A stronger convergence or remote-homology conclusion requires independent evidence: global domain-level structural alignment and matching topology, sequence correspondence across the structural core, motifs compared at equivalent structural positions, compatible domain context, and phylogenetic or literature support. Ligand-bound structures plus biochemical, kinetic, and mutational evidence are needed for cofactor orientation, specificity, and catalytic-function transfer. No best representative or template follows from these classifications; that would require correct domain boundaries, structural coverage and state, ligand relevance, and quality records for every candidate rather than hierarchy alone.

prompt: How did the relationship between the ColG collagenase domain in PDB 1nqd and the Cry3A C-terminal domain in PDB 1dlc change from SCOPe 2.04 to current SCOPe, and what structural and functional evidence supports their common ancestry?
answer:
In SCOPe 2.04, the ColG collagen-binding domain d1nqda_ (SUNID 86025) was b.23.2.1: CUB-like fold b.23, collagen-binding-domain superfamily b.23.2. Cry3A domain d1dlca1 (SUNID 23719; residues A:500–644) was b.18.1.3: galactose-binding-domain-like fold b.18 and superfamily b.18.1. Their deepest shared node was therefore only the all-beta class b (SUNID 48724), so 2.04 made no positive homology assertion between them.

The current public stable release is 2.08, and the latest periodic overlay, 2.08-2026-08-16, returns the same relationship. ColG was moved to b.18.1.36, while Cry3A remains b.18.1.3. They now share fold b.18 and, importantly, superfamily b.18.1 (SUNID 49785), supporting probable common ancestry. They remain separate families—ColG collagen-binding domain b.18.1.36 (SUNID 267607) versus delta-endotoxin C-terminal domain b.18.1.3 (SUNID 49796)—so this is remote superfamily-level homology, not close family-level equivalence.

Structural evidence is consistent with that reassignment. The ColG-family SCOPe annotation cites PMID 17977833 as describing likely homology among a ColG CBD (d1nqdb_), a Cry toxin C-terminal domain (Cry4Ba d1w99a3, also family b.18.1.3), and the CPE C-terminal domain d2quoa_. In the stored FATCAT evidence, 1nqdA itself maps to the near-identical representative 1nqjA (99.16% identity over 119 alignment columns); that representative matches d1w99a3 with P=0.00395 and RMSD 2.52 Å despite only 2.5% sequence identity. This is indirect family-bridging evidence rather than a retrieved direct 1nqd–1dlc superposition, but it supports preservation of the all-beta, galactose-binding-domain-like core after sequence divergence.

The functional theme is also compatible with divergence from a binding-module ancestor: the ColG domain is a noncatalytic collagen-binding module, whereas Cry3A domain III is a C-terminal target/receptor-recognition and specificity module of an insecticidal toxin. Both recruit a larger bacterial effector to a macromolecular target, but that broad similarity is supporting context, not proof by itself. Collagen specificity, calcium-associated properties, Cry receptor/glycan specificity, insecticidal activity, and pore-forming mechanism must not be transferred between the families. Their low sequence identity and family-specific loops also make them non-interchangeable templates for binding-site or ligand-specific modeling; template use should be limited to the conserved structural core unless a direct alignment supports more.

SCOPe exposes the classification, a literature pointer, and representative FATCAT evidence, but not the paper’s full alignment or experiments. Stronger claims about the exact evolutionary path or conserved binding mechanism require a direct 1nqd–1dlc structural superposition and residue correspondence, sensitive sequence/profile and phylogenetic evidence, ligand/receptor-bound structures, domain-context analysis, and biochemical binding or mutational experiments.

prompt: d1p7jd_ and d1ztra1 share homeodomain family a.4.1.1, but d1ztra1 has an hf annotation. What remains justified about homology, and why should the structures not be treated as interchangeable templates or training examples?
answer:
In SCOPe 2.08 (stable label 2.08-stable), d1p7jd_ (SUNID 94286) and d1ztra1 (SUNID 125655) have the same lineage through Homeodomain-like superfamily a.4.1 (SUNID 46689) and Homeodomain family a.4.1.1 (SUNID 46690). The shared family remains positive SCOPe evidence of a close evolutionary relationship/common ancestry; d1ztra1’s hf annotation qualifies structural uniformity but does not erase that homology inference.

The hf record says that d1ztra1 adopts a fold different from the exemplar domain despite similar sequence and number of secondary structures. It does not, without a direct comparison, establish exactly how d1ztra1 differs from d1p7jd_ or even that d1p7jd_ is the referenced exemplar. Nevertheless, it makes an ordinary same-family assumption of interchangeable folds unsafe. One must not transfer topology, residue correspondence, secondary-structure packing, coordinates, DNA/ligand-binding geometry, conformational state, mutation effects, or detailed function between them solely from a.4.1.1 membership. SCOPe also records both as mutants and comments that d1p7jd_ is “complexed with nhe,” so their recorded construct/context is not identical.

They are likewise unsuitable as unqualified interchangeable training examples. Because they share a family, placing one in training and the other in a nominally independent test set can leak close evolutionary information; conversely, treating the hf structure as a negative-homology example would contradict the family-level evidence. A homogeneous-fold dataset should exclude or stratify the hf case, preserve its annotation, control sequence redundancy, and report a sensitivity analysis; a heterogeneity-focused dataset may retain it as an explicitly labeled exception.

Stronger template or transfer claims require a direct pairwise structural alignment/superposition with topology and residue mapping, sequence alignment with identity and coverage, construct/mutation and domain-context comparison, ligand- or DNA-bound structural evidence, and biochemical or literature evidence for any claimed functional equivalence. Those data were not supplied by the retrieved hierarchy and caveat records.

prompt: d1uc6a1 and d1o5dt2 belong to fibronectin type III family b.1.2.1, but d1o5dt2 is annotated as a fragment. How should that annotation affect alignment, representative selection, and interpretation of family diversity?
answer:
In SCOPe 2.08, d1uc6a1 (SUNID 107766; 1uc6 A:6-109) and d1o5dt2 (SUNID 103884; 1o5d T:107-205) share family b.1.2.1, Fibronectin type III (SUNID 49266), within superfamily b.1.2, fold b.1, and class b. This family-level placement supports a close evolutionary relationship, but d1o5dt2 has the domain-specific `fr` annotation: “fragment; missing more than one-third of the common structure and/or sequence.”

Alignment should therefore be coverage-aware and restricted to the reliably corresponding structural core. Unobserved or omitted parts of d1o5dt2 must be treated as missing data, not as genuine family insertions/deletions, topology changes, or sequence divergence. Report aligned coverage alongside identity or similarity and avoid comparing unnormalized global scores as if both domains were complete.

For representative selection, the fragment should not be the sole canonical representative of a complete fibronectin type III domain or a full-domain modeling template. Its retained core may still be useful for local alignment, fragment modeling, or its observed complex state. Between these entries, the fragment flag argues against choosing d1o5dt2 as the default full-family representative, but it does not by itself prove d1uc6a1 is optimal or complete. Technical quality must be considered separately: 1o5d has higher SPACI/AEROSPACI (0.28747195) than 1uc6 (0.02158265), while 1o5d is a 2.05-Å X-ray structure and 1uc6 is NMR; neither R factor is available. Those quality values cannot compensate for missing family coverage, and the differing methods preclude a simple resolution-only ranking. A representative set should verify construct completeness and preferably retain a complete-domain structure plus d1o5dt2 as a separately labeled fragment/complex example when biologically relevant.

The fragment must not inflate apparent family diversity: missing elements are not evidence of a naturally shorter fibronectin type III architecture. Nor does shared family membership make the functions of ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor alpha (the d1uc6a1 protein node) and extracellular human tissue factor (the d1o5dt2 protein node) interchangeable. Transferring ligand specificity, receptor activity, interaction partners, or whole-protein function requires full-length sequence and construct mapping, coverage-qualified structural alignment, domain-context evidence, and ligand-bound or biochemical data. Full-domain template use likewise requires verified target coverage and preferably an additional complete-domain structure.

prompt: A newly solved domain resembles a known SCOPe fold but lacks convincing evidence of common ancestry with any existing superfamily. Should it be assigned to a new family, a new superfamily in the existing fold, or a new fold? What biological claim does each choice make?
answer:
Conditionally assign it as a new superfamily within the existing fold, provided a domain-level structural comparison confirms the fold’s major secondary-structure arrangement and topology. This records fold-level structural similarity while making no SCOPe assertion of common ancestry between the new domain and existing superfamilies.

A new family would have to sit within a superfamily. It would therefore assert probable common ancestry with that superfamily’s other families, while identifying the new family as a distinct, closer subgroup. The stated lack of convincing ancestry evidence makes that choice unjustified.

A new superfamily in the existing fold says that its members are hypothesized to share an evolutionary origin with one another, but SCOPe does not assert homology to the fold’s other superfamilies. Separate superfamilies do not prove nonhomology, analogy, convergence, or independent origin.

A new fold claims that the domain has a materially different overall arrangement/topology, not merely that homology is undetectable. It is appropriate only if detailed structural comparison shows the resemblance to the known fold is insufficient. A new fold is likewise a structural classification, not proof of an independent evolutionary origin.

The decision requires a global structural alignment and topology comparison. A stronger ancestry claim additionally needs evidence such as sequence correspondence across equivalent core positions, conserved motifs in equivalent structural contexts, compatible domain architecture and biological context, phylogenetic support, or relevant literature/experiments. Fold membership alone cannot safely transfer exact function, substrate, reaction, ligand preference, mechanism, oligomeric state, or whole-protein annotation. An existing-fold structure may be a cautious core-topology template, but interchangeable-template use—especially for loops, insertions, active sites, and ligand geometry—requires direct alignment and functional evidence.

The public API reports SCOPe 2.08 (stable label 2.08-stable) as the current stable release. Because the domain and fold are hypothetical and unnamed, no release-specific SID, SUNID, SCCS, boundary, or actual placement can be verified.

prompt: Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases, and phosphoinositide 3-kinases have related catalytic-domain architecture in SCOPe. What common evolutionary or mechanistic conclusions are justified, and what evidence is needed before transferring substrate specificity or regulation?
answer:
In stable SCOPe 2.08, the three catalytic-domain groups are separate families within the same Protein kinase-like superfamily, d.144.1 (SUNID 56112), and fold d.144 (SUNID 56111): phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic domains are d.144.1.4 (SUNID 56171), aminoglycoside/APH phosphotransferases are d.144.1.6 (SUNID 64411), and canonical protein-kinase catalytic subunits are d.144.1.7 (SUNID 88854). Sharing a superfamily—not merely a fold—supports probable common ancestry of their catalytic domains and a conserved kinase-like structural core. Their names and architecture are consistent with a broad ATP-dependent phosphoryl-transfer strategy, but the retrieved hierarchy alone does not demonstrate identical catalytic residues, metal requirements, transition-state chemistry, or evolutionary direction.

The distinct families mark substantial specialization. It is unsafe to transfer canonical protein- or peptide-substrate specificity to APHs or PI3Ks, aminoglycoside specificity or antibiotic-resistance phenotype to the other groups, or phosphoinositide head-group specificity to protein kinases or APHs. Likewise, activation-loop control, regulatory phosphorylation, autoinhibition, regulatory-subunit binding, membrane recruitment, localization, allostery, inhibitor sensitivity, kinetics, and whole-protein pathway roles cannot be transferred across these families from superfamily membership. SCOPe classifies domains; adjacent regulatory domains and full-length architectures may differ.

Stronger mechanistic or functional transfer requires domain-level sequence alignments establishing correspondence of nucleotide-, metal-, catalytic-, and substrate-contacting residues; quantitative structural alignments; structures in relevant ATP/ADP, metal, native-substrate, product, inhibitor, and conformational states; biochemical substrate panels, binding and kinetic measurements, and mutational validation. Regulatory transfer additionally requires full-length/domain-context evidence, regulatory-partner and interface structures, post-translational-modification data, membrane/lipid-context studies where relevant, cellular assays, phylogenetic analysis, and supporting literature.

A member of another d.144.1 family may be a remote-homology or conserved-core template, but it is not an interchangeable template for substrate-binding loops, inserts, regulatory interfaces, or active-state modeling. Prefer family-matched templates with the required ligand, conformation, and domain context. No best representative can be selected from hierarchy alone; structural-quality records would have to be compared for every candidate, and SPACI/AEROSPACI would assess technical quality rather than functional equivalence.
